title: ISC U1·W2 — IT General Controls & Application Controls in Depth (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the two layers of IT control

Within the governed IT environment from Week 1 sit two layers of control: IT general controls (ITGCs) that govern the whole environment, and application controls that operate inside a specific process. AUD Unit 3 introduced these from the auditor's chair; ISC examines them from the systems-and-controls designer's chair — deeper, with the access, change, and processing mechanics that make Meridian Building Group's data complete, accurate, and authorized. This week is the technical core of the discipline.

The four ITGC domains

ITGCs fall into four domains. Access to programs and data (logical and physical security) restricts who can see and change what. Program change management controls how software is modified, tested, and approved before production. Program development governs acquiring and implementing new systems. Computer operations covers job scheduling, backup, and recovery. These pervasive controls are the foundation: if any is weak, the application controls that depend on it cannot be relied upon — a programmer with uncontrolled production access can defeat any automated edit check.

Access control — authentication

Access control begins with authentication — proving identity through something you know (a password), have (a token or phone), or are (a biometric). Combining factors yields multi-factor authentication (MFA), far stronger than a password alone. Strong authentication policies (password complexity, rotation, lockout after failed attempts) and protected credential storage are the first line of defense. Authentication answers "who are you?" before the system decides what you may do.

Access control — authorization and accountability

After authentication comes authorization — what the authenticated user may do — governed by the principle of least privilege (grant only the access needed for the role) and implemented through role-based access control (RBAC). Privileged (administrator) access is tightly restricted and monitored. Finally, accountability requires logging of who did what and when, with logs reviewed for anomalies. The trio — authentication, authorization, accountability — is the backbone of logical security, and weaknesses here are the most common and serious IT control deficiencies.

Physical access and environmental controls

Logical controls mean little if someone can walk to a server. Physical access controls — badge readers, locked data centers, visitor logs, cameras — protect the hardware, while environmental controls (fire suppression, climate control, uninterruptible power) protect against non-malicious threats. For cloud-hosted systems these controls shift to the provider and are evidenced through its SOC reports. Physical and environmental controls complete the access picture: the data must be safe from both unauthorized users and physical harm.

Change management and program development

Change management ensures software changes are authorized, tested, approved, and documented before reaching production, with development, test, and production environments kept separate and migration performed by someone other than the developer. Emergency changes follow an expedited but still-controlled path with after-the-fact review. Program development applies the same discipline to new systems through the systems development life cycle (next week). Together they prevent unauthorized or untested code — the change that silently breaks a control or corrupts data — from entering live systems.

Application controls by stage

Application controls ensure a specific process produces complete, accurate, authorized results, classified by stage. Input controls validate data at entry — edit checks, field/format checks, check digits, validity and limit/reasonableness tests, and self-checking of key fields. Processing controls ensure correct handling — batch totals, hash totals, run-to-run reconciliations, and sequence checks. Output controls govern the results — distribution restrictions, output reconciliation, and error reporting. A well-designed application catches a bad transaction at input rather than discovering it in the financial statements.

Classifying controls

Controls are also classified by function and nature. By function: preventive (stop an error before it happens — an edit check), detective (find an error that occurred — a reconciliation), and corrective (fix it — a backup restore). By nature: manual versus automated. The strongest control environments favor preventive, automated controls (consistent and hard to bypass) backed by detective controls that catch what slips through. Mapping each control to its type helps a designer or auditor see whether a process is genuinely protected or merely appears to be.

The CIA triad

Information security is organized around the CIA triad — confidentiality (only authorized parties can read the data), integrity (the data is accurate and unaltered), and availability (the data and systems are accessible when needed). Every control maps to one or more of these objectives: encryption protects confidentiality, hash totals and input edits protect integrity, and backups and redundancy protect availability. The triad gives a designer a checklist — a control that strengthens confidentiality may do nothing for availability — and it frames the security, confidentiality, and privacy content the ISC discipline tests in depth.

Network and boundary controls

Beyond user access, controls protect the perimeter and the data in transit. Firewalls filter traffic between networks; intrusion detection/prevention systems watch for and block attacks; network segmentation and a demilitarized zone (DMZ) isolate public-facing systems from internal ones; and encryption protects data both in transit (TLS) and at rest. Endpoint protections (anti-malware, device management) defend the many access points a modern organization exposes. These boundary controls are general controls in the broadest sense — they protect the environment within which every application and its data operate.

Backup, recovery, and operations controls

The fourth ITGC domain — computer operations — keeps systems running and recoverable. Backups are taken on a defined schedule, stored offsite (or in a separate cloud region), and periodically tested by restoring them, because an untested backup is only a hope. Job scheduling and monitoring ensure batch processes run completely and in order, and incident management logs and resolves failures. A documented disaster-recovery plan defines recovery-time and recovery-point objectives, and capacity monitoring keeps systems available before demand outstrips resources. These operations controls protect availability and integrity: when a server fails or data is corrupted, a tested backup and a recovery procedure are what stand between a brief disruption and a catastrophe — the corrective controls behind the preventive and detective ones.

CMA bridge

When MBG's system rejects a job-cost entry with an invalid cost code, that is an input control doing its job; when month-end batch totals reconcile, that is a processing control. The CFO's confidence in system-generated reports rests on exactly these general and application controls — the difference between data that is trustworthy and data that merely exists.

Practice and recap

  1. Know the four ITGC domains: access to programs/data, change management, program development, computer operations.
  2. Apply access control: authentication (know/have/are, MFA), authorization (least privilege, RBAC), accountability (logging), plus physical/environmental controls.
  3. Enforce change management: authorize/test/approve, separate dev/test/production, migrate via someone other than the developer.
  4. Classify application controls by stage (input edit/validity/limit checks; processing batch/hash totals/reconciliations; output controls) and by function (preventive/detective/corrective; manual/automated).

Recap: ITGCs span access, change management, development, and operations and make application controls reliable; access control rests on authentication (something you know/have/are, MFA), authorization (least privilege, RBAC), and accountability (logging), backed by physical and environmental controls; change management authorizes, tests, approves, and segregates environments so untested code never reaches production; and application controls operate by stage (input edit/check-digit/limit tests, processing batch/hash totals and reconciliations, output controls) and by function (preventive, detective, corrective), with automated preventive controls the strongest.

flashcards.back: Access to programs and data, program change management, program development, and computer operations. Weak ITGCs undermine the application controls that rely on them.
Something you KNOW (password), HAVE (token/phone), or ARE (biometric). Combining them = multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Authorization grants only the access a role needs (least privilege), implemented via role-based access control; privileged access is restricted and monitored.
Who are you? (authenticate) → what may you do? (authorize) → what did you do? (accountability via logging). The backbone of logical security.
Authorize, test, approve, and document changes; keep dev/test/production separate; migrate to production via someone other than the developer.
Input (edit/format/check-digit/validity/limit checks), Processing (batch/hash totals, reconciliations, sequence checks), Output (distribution, reconciliation, error reports).
Preventive (stop before — edit check), Detective (find after — reconciliation), Corrective (fix — backup restore). Plus manual vs automated.
Preventive + automated controls (consistent, hard to bypass), backed by detective controls to catch what slips through.

questions.q: A check digit appended to an account number is a(n):
questions.explain: Check digits validate data at entry — an input application control.

choices: Two or more of: something you know, have, or are
questions.explain: MFA combines factors of different types (know/have/are), far stronger than a single password.

questions.q: The principle of least privilege means:
choices: Granting only the access a role requires
questions.explain: Least privilege limits each user to the minimum access needed for their role.

questions.q: Good change management requires that production migration be performed by:
choices: Someone other than the developer who wrote the change
questions.explain: Separating development from production migration prevents unauthorized or untested code from going live.

questions.q: Batch totals reconciled before and after processing are a(n):
questions.explain: Batch and hash totals reconciled across processing are processing controls.

questions.q: A reconciliation that detects an error after it has occurred is a:
questions.explain: Detective controls find errors that occurred; preventive controls stop them beforehand.

questions.q: If IT general controls over access are weak, the auditor or designer should:
choices: Not rely on automated application controls without further work
questions.explain: Application controls depend on ITGCs; weak access control undermines reliance on automated controls.
